title: Chapter 14
paragraphs: But at that very moment the princess walked in. There was a look of horror on her face when she saw them alone and saw their disturbed expressions. Levin bowed to her and said nothing. Kitty did not speak or look up. "Thank God, she has refused him," the mother thought, and her face lit up with the habitual smile she greeted her Thursday guests with. She sat down and began questioning Levin about his life in the country. He sat down again as well, waiting for other visitors to arrive so that he could slip out unnoticed.
Five minutes later in came a friend of Kitty's, married the previous winter, Countess Nordston.

She was a thin, sallow, sickly, and nervous woman with brilliant black eyes. She was fond of Kitty, and her affection for her showed itself, as the affection of married women for girls always does, in the wish to make a match for Kitty after her own ideal of married happiness; she wanted her to marry Vronsky. Levin she had often met at the Shtcherbatskys' earlier in the winter, and she had always disliked him. Her unvarying favorite occupation when they met was poking fun at him.

"I do love it when he looks down on me from the height of his grandeur, or breaks off his learned conversation with me because I'm a fool, or is condescending. I love that — seeing him condescending! I'm so glad he can't bear me," she used to say of him.

She was right, for Levin really could not bear her, and despised her for what she was proud of and considered a fine trait — her nervousness, her delicate contempt and indifference for everything coarse and earthly.

Countess Nordston and Levin had fallen into the sort of relationship not infrequently seen in society, in which two people who remain outwardly on friendly terms despise each other so thoroughly that they cannot even take each other seriously, cannot even be offended by each other.
Countess Nordston pounced on Levin at once.

"Ah, Konstantin Dmitrievitch! So you've come back to our corrupt Babylon," she said, giving him her tiny yellow hand and recalling that he had happened to say earlier in the winter that Moscow was a Babylon. "Tell me, has Babylon been reformed, or have you degenerated?" she added, glancing at Kitty with a smirk.

"It's very flattering for me, countess, that you remember my words so well," Levin replied, having managed to recover his composure and from habit dropping at once into his tone of joking hostility toward Countess Nordston. "They must certainly make a great impression on you."
"Oh, I should think so. I always note them all down. Well, Kitty, have you been skating again?"

And she began talking to Kitty. Awkward as it would be for Levin to leave now, it would still have been easier than staying the whole evening and watching Kitty, who glanced at him every now and then and avoided his eyes. He was on the point of getting up when the princess, noticing that he was silent, addressed him.
"Will you be in Moscow long? But you're busy with the district council, aren't you, so you can't be away for long?"
"No, princess, I'm no longer a member of the council," he said. "I've come up for a few days."

"There's something the matter with him," Countess Nordston thought, glancing at his stern, serious face. "He's not in his old argumentative mood. But I'll draw him out. I do love making a fool of him in front of Kitty, and I will."

"Konstantin Dmitrievitch," she said to him, "do explain to me, please, what's the meaning of this. You know all about these things. At home in our village of Kaluga all the peasants and all the women have drunk up everything they had, and now they can't pay us any rent. What's the meaning of that? You're always praising the peasants so."
At that instant another lady came into the room, and Levin got up.
"Excuse me, countess, but I really know nothing about it and can't tell you anything," he said, and glanced at the officer who had come in behind the lady.

"That must be Vronsky," Levin thought, and to be sure of it he glanced at Kitty. She had already had time to look at Vronsky and was now glancing at Levin. And simply from the look in her eyes, which had grown unconsciously brighter, Levin knew that she loved that man, knew it as surely as if she had told him so in words. But what kind of man was he? Now, for better or worse, Levin could not help staying; he had to find out what the man she loved was like.

There are people who, on meeting a successful rival, no matter in what, are at once inclined to turn their backs on everything good in him and to see only what is bad. There are others, on the other hand, who want above all to find in that lucky rival the qualities by which he has outstripped them, and who go looking, with an aching heart, only for what is good. Levin belonged to the second sort. But he had no difficulty in finding what was good and attractive in Vronsky. It was obvious at first glance. Vronsky was a squarely built, dark-haired man, not very tall, with a good-humored, handsome, and unusually calm and resolute face. Everything about his face and figure, from his short-cropped black hair and freshly shaven chin to his loosely fitting, brand-new uniform, was simple and at the same time elegant. Making way for the lady who had just come in, Vronsky went up to the princess and then to Kitty.

As he came up to her, his beautiful eyes shone with a particularly tender light, and with a faint, happy, modestly triumphant smile (so it looked to Levin), he bowed carefully and respectfully over her, and reached out his small, broad hand.
Greeting and saying a few words to everyone, he sat down without once glancing at Levin, who had not taken his eyes off him.
"Let me introduce you," said the princess, indicating Levin. "Konstantin Dmitrievitch Levin, Count Alexey Kirillovitch Vronsky."
Vronsky got up and, looking cordially at Levin, shook his hand.
"I believe I was supposed to have dined with you this winter," he said, smiling his simple, open smile; "but you unexpectedly left for the country."
"Konstantin Dmitrievitch despises and hates town and us townspeople," said Countess Nordston.
"My words must make a deep impression on you, since you remember them so well," said Levin, and, suddenly aware that he had just said the same thing before, he reddened.
Vronsky looked at Levin and Countess Nordston and smiled.
"Are you always in the country?" he inquired. "I should think it must be dull in winter."
"It isn't dull if you have work to do; besides, one isn't dull alone," Levin replied curtly.
"I'm fond of the country," said Vronsky, noticing — and pretending not to notice — Levin's tone.
"But I hope, count, you wouldn't agree to live in the country always," said Countess Nordston.

"I don't know; I've never tried it for long. I had an odd feeling once," he went on. "I never longed so for the country, the Russian countryside, with bast shoes and peasants, as when I was spending a winter with my mother in Nice. Nice itself is dull enough, you know. And really, Naples and Sorrento are only pleasant for a short time. And it's just there that Russia comes back to me most vividly, and especially the country. It's as though..."
He kept talking, addressing both Kitty and Levin in turn, his serene, friendly eyes moving from one to the other, and clearly saying whatever happened to come into his head.
Noticing that Countess Nordston wanted to say something, he stopped short without finishing what he had begun and listened to her attentively.

The conversation did not flag for a moment, so that the princess, who always kept in reserve, in case the conversation should run out, two heavy guns — the relative merits of classical and modern education, and universal military service — did not have to bring out either of them, and Countess Nordston had no chance to tease Levin.
Levin wanted to join in the general conversation but could not; saying to himself every minute, "Now go," he still did not go, as though waiting for something.
The conversation turned to table-turning and spirits, and Countess Nordston, who believed in spiritualism, began describing the marvels she had seen.
"Ah, countess, you simply must take me — for pity's sake, do take me to see them. I've never seen anything out of the ordinary, though I'm always on the lookout," Vronsky said, smiling.
"Very well — next Saturday," Countess Nordston answered. "But you, Konstantin Dmitrievitch, do you believe in it?" she asked Levin.
"Why are you asking me? You know what I'll say."
"But I want to hear your opinion."

"My opinion," Levin answered, "is just that this table-turning simply proves that what is called educated society is no higher than the peasants. They believe in the evil eye, and in witchcraft and omens, while we..."
"Oh, so you don't believe in it?"
"I can't believe in it, countess."
"But if I've seen it myself?"
"The peasant women tell us they have seen goblins."
"So you think I'm lying?"
And she gave a mirthless laugh.

"Oh no, Masha, Konstantin Dmitrievitch said he couldn't believe in it," said Kitty, blushing for Levin; Levin saw this, and, still more exasperated, would have answered, but Vronsky, with his bright, open smile, rushed to the rescue of a conversation that was threatening to become unpleasant.
"You don't admit the possibility at all?" he asked. "Why not? We accept the existence of electricity, of which we know nothing. Why shouldn't there be some new force, still unknown to us, which..."

"When electricity was discovered," Levin cut in quickly, "only the phenomenon was discovered; what produced it and what its effects might be were unknown, and ages passed before any practical uses for it were thought of. But the spiritualists have started with tables writing for them and spirits appearing to them, and only afterwards begun to say that it is some unknown force."
Vronsky listened to Levin attentively, as he always did, obviously interested in what he was saying.

"Yes, but what the spiritualists say is: we don't yet know what this force is, but a force exists, and these are the conditions under which it acts. Let the scientists work out what the force consists of. No, I don't see why a new force shouldn't exist, if it..."

"Because with electricity," Levin interrupted again, "every time you rub tar against wool, a recognized phenomenon appears, but in this case it doesn't happen every time, and so it isn't a natural phenomenon at all."

Feeling, presumably, that the conversation was taking too serious a tone for a drawing-room, Vronsky offered no rejoinder, but, by way of trying to change the subject, smiled brightly and turned to the ladies.
"Let's try it right now, countess," he said; but Levin meant to finish saying what he thought.

"I think," he went on, "that this attempt by the spiritualists to explain their wonders as some new natural force is utterly pointless. They boldly talk of spiritual force, and then try to subject it to material experiment."
Everyone was waiting for him to finish, and he felt it.
"And I think you would be a first-rate medium," said Countess Nordston; "there's something enthusiastic in you."
Levin opened his mouth, was about to say something, reddened, and said nothing.
"Let's try table-turning right now, please," Vronsky said. "Princess, will you allow it?"
And Vronsky stood up, looking for a small table.

Kitty got up to fetch a table, and as she passed her eyes met Levin's. She felt for him with her whole heart, the more so because she was pitying him for suffering of which she herself was the cause. "If you can forgive me, forgive me," her eyes said; "I am so happy."

"I hate them all, and you, and myself," his eyes answered, and he picked up his hat. But he was not to escape. Just as they were arranging themselves around the table, and Levin was on the point of leaving, the old prince came in, and after greeting the ladies turned to Levin.

"Ah!" he began with delight. "Been here long, my boy? I didn't even know you were in town. Very glad to see you." The old prince embraced Levin, and while talking to him did not notice Vronsky, who had risen and was waiting calmly for the prince to turn to him.

Kitty felt how distasteful her father's warmth was to Levin after what had just happened. She also saw how coldly her father at last acknowledged Vronsky's bow, and how Vronsky looked at her father with amiable bewilderment, as if trying and failing to understand how and why anyone could be hostile toward him, and she flushed.
"Prince, let us have Konstantin Dmitrievitch," said Countess Nordston; "we want to try an experiment."

"What experiment? Table-turning? Well, you must excuse me, ladies and gentlemen, but to my mind it's better fun to play the ring game," said the old prince, looking at Vronsky and guessing that the idea had been his. "There's some sense in that, at least."
Vronsky looked at the prince in surprise with his resolute eyes and, with a faint smile, at once began talking to Countess Nordston about the great ball that was coming up next week.

"I hope you'll be there?" he said to Kitty. As soon as the old prince turned away from him, Levin slipped out unnoticed, and the last impression he carried away of that evening was the smiling, happy face of Kitty answering Vronsky's question about the ball.
